label: Person
name: Moses
summary:
Moses (c. 1391–1271 BCE, traditional dating) was the Hebrew prophet, lawgiver, and liberator who led the Israelites out of Egyptian bondage (the Exodus), received the Torah on Mount Sinai, and established the covenant relationship between God and Israel that defines Judaism.

Found as an infant in a basket on the Nile and raised in Pharaoh's household, he fled after killing an Egyptian taskmaster. At the burning bush (Exodus 3), God commissioned him to confront Pharaoh and deliver Israel. The ten plagues — climaxing in the death of the firstborn and the first Passover — compelled Pharaoh to release the Israelites.

At Sinai, Moses received the Ten Commandments and the Torah — the foundational legal, ethical, and ritual code of Judaism. He mediated between God and Israel for 40 years of wilderness wandering, organizing twelve tribes into a nation.

He died within sight of the Promised Land on Mount Nebo. Judaism, Christianity, and Islam honor him as prophet. Western legal tradition from Roman law through the Magna Carta traces its ethical foundations to the Mosaic code.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Moses led the Israelites out of Egyptian bondage and received the Torah on Mount Sinai, establishing a covenant relationship between God and Israel that defines Judaism. This event had significant regional impact in the ancient Near East.

causes: Enslavement of the Israelites in Egypt under Pharaoh's forced labor corvée, creating the conditions for a national deliverance narrative
God's covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Genesis 15:13-14) that prophesied 400 years of affliction followed by liberation with great possessions
Pharaoh's decree to drown Hebrew male infants, which paradoxically placed Moses in the Egyptian royal household
effects: Establishment of the Torah as the foundational legal code of Western civilization — the first comprehensive written law binding ruler and citizen alike under divine authority
Institution of Passover (Pesach), the oldest continuously observed religious festival in the Abrahamic tradition
Creation of the Tabernacle worship system and Aaronic priesthood that structured Israelite religion for over a millennium
The Exodus narrative became the archetypal liberation story — inspiring the Maccabean revolt, American Revolution, abolitionist movement, and Civil Rights Movement
Transmission of monotheistic theology from covenantal promise to codified national religion, shaping Judaism, Christianity, and Islam
The concept of a supreme written constitution binding both governed and governors — foundational to Western constitutional thought

relationships.context: Moses fulfilled the covenant promise made to Abraham in Genesis 15:13-14 by liberating Israel from Egypt
Moses consecrated Aaron as the first High Priest in a seven-day ordination ceremony at Mount Sinai (Exodus 29)
Moses established the hereditary Aaronic priesthood under God's instruction
Moses oversaw construction of the Ark at God's specification (Exodus 25:10-22)
Traditionally credited as author of the Pentateuch (Five Books of Moses)
Central to Israelite national identity from the Exodus through the monarchy
Exodus 1-40 narrates Moses' life from birth through the Tabernacle's completion
Numbers records the 40-year wilderness journey under Moses' leadership
Moses as mediator of the old covenant prefigures Christ as mediator of the new covenant (Hebrews 3:1-6)
Born and raised in Egypt; the Exodus is the defining event of Egyptian-Israelite relations
